questions.prompt: The free response of \(\dot{x} = Ax\) from initial state \(x(0)\) is
questions.explanation: The matrix exponential \(e^{At}\) generalizes the scalar exponential. It multiplies the initial state to give the state at time \(t\). \(Ax(0)\) is a single derivative, not the time evolution. \(x(0) + At\) is a linear ramp. \(x(0)e^{-t}\) assumes a specific eigenvalue of \(-1\).
questions.figure_alt: A curve that decays toward zero.

questions.prompt: A one-state system has \(\dot{x} = -0.5 x\). From \(x(0) = 4\), the state at \(t = 2\) is
questions.explanation: \(x(t) = e^{-0.5 t} x(0) = e^{-1} \times 4 = 1.472\). The eigenvalue is \(-0.5\), so the decay is slower than \(e^{-t}\). Using \(e^{-2}\) instead of \(e^{-1}\) squares the exponent.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that decays toward zero.

questions.prompt: A diagonal \(A\) has eigenvalues \(-1\) and \(-3\). The slower mode decays with time constant
questions.explanation: The time constant is \(1/|\lambda|\). The slower mode is \(\lambda = -1\), so \(\tau = 1\) s. The \(-3\) mode has \(\tau = 1/3\). Adding the eigenvalues gives \(-4\), which is not a time constant.

questions.prompt: Starting from \(x_1(0) = 1\), \(x_2(0) = 0\), the decoupled system \(\dot{x}_1 = -2x_1\), \(\dot{x}_2 = -4x_2\) has \(x_1(1)\) equal to
questions.explanation: The first state evolves as \(x_1(t) = e^{-2t}\). At \(t = 1\), that is \(e^{-2} = 0.135\). The second state stays at zero because its initial condition is zero. Using \(e^{-4}\) applies the wrong eigenvalue.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that decays toward zero.

questions.prompt: The matrix exponential of a diagonal matrix \(\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2)\) is
questions.explanation: The exponential of a diagonal matrix is the diagonal of the exponentials. Each mode evolves independently. The sum of eigenvalues in the exponent would collapse the two modes into one; that is wrong. A linear term \(\lambda t\) is not an exponential. The original matrix without time evolution is missing the \(t\) dependence.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>diagonal exponential</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">e^{λ₁t}   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   e^{λ₂t}</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 diagonal matrix of exponentials.

questions.prompt: An eigenvalue is \(-4\). The time for that mode to decay to \(e^{-1}\) of its initial value is
questions.explanation: One time constant is \(\tau = 1/4 = 0.25\) s. At that time the exponential is \(e^{-4 \times 0.25} = e^{-1}\). Using the eigenvalue itself as the time gives \(e^{-16}\), which is far too small.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>one real eigenvalue</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="48" y2="90"/><line x1="76" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="57" y1="85" x2="67" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="57" y1="95" x2="67" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: One pole mark on the negative real axis.

questions.prompt: Two eigenvalues are \(-2\) and \(-6\). The state after 10 time constants of the slower mode is dominated by
questions.explanation: After many time constants the faster mode is negligible. The slower eigenvalue \(-2\) dominates. The \(-6\) mode dies in about \(10/6 = 1.67\) s while the \(-2\) mode takes 5 s to decay by \(e^{-10}\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>slow and fast modes</title><line x1="32" y1="90" x2="92" y2="90"/><line x1="120" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="101" y1="85" x2="111" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="101" y1="95" x2="111" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="13" y1="85" x2="23" y2="95" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="13" y1="95" x2="23" y2="85" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Pole marks on the negative real axis.

questions.prompt: If all eigenvalues of \(A\) have negative real parts, the free response
questions.explanation: Every mode is a decaying exponential times a sinusoid (or just the exponential for real eigenvalues). All modes die out, so the state decays to zero. Right-half eigenvalues would grow. Purely imaginary eigenvalues would oscillate forever. A constant state would need an eigenvalue at zero.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>stable complex pair</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="123" y1="41" x2="133" y2="51" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="123" y1="51" x2="133" y2="41" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="123" y1="129" x2="133" y2="139" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="123" y1="139" x2="133" y2="129" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Two pole marks in the left half-plane.

questions.prompt: A complex eigenvalue is \(-1 + 2j\). The envelope of that mode decays with time constant
questions.explanation: The envelope decays as \(e^{-|\mathrm{Re}(\lambda)|t} = e^{-t}\), so \(\tau = 1\) s. The imaginary part 2 sets the oscillation frequency, not the decay rate. Using 2 as the time constant confuses oscillation with decay.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>complex pair</title><line x1="20" y1="90" x2="280" y2="90"/><polygon points="280,90 273.6,92.7 273.6,87.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="160" x2="150" y2="16"/><polygon points="150,16 152.7,22.4 147.3,22.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="274" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Re</text><text x="158" y="14" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">Im</text><line x1="123" y1="41" x2="133" y2="51" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="123" y1="51" x2="133" y2="41" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="123" y1="129" x2="133" y2="139" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="123" y1="139" x2="133" y2="129" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Two pole marks forming a conjugate pair.

questions.prompt: For mode analysis: a diagonal \(A\) has entries \(-0.5\) and \(-2\). From \(x(0) = [1, 1]^T\), the value of \(x_2\) at \(t = 1\) is
questions.explanation: \(x_2(t) = e^{-2t} x_2(0) = e^{-2}\). The first state uses \(-0.5\), but this question asks about the second. Mixing the eigenvalues gives \(e^{-0.5}\), which is the first component.

questions.prompt: A 3-by-3 realization of a transfer function has eigenvalues \(-1\), \(-2\), \(-5\). The slowest mode has time constant
questions.explanation: The slowest eigenvalue is \(-1\), so \(\tau = 1\) s. The \(-2\) mode has \(\tau = 0.5\) s and the \(-5\) mode has \(\tau = 0.2\) s. The sum of eigenvalues is not a time constant.

questions.prompt: An LTI system is stable when
questions.explanation: Every eigenvalue in the open left half-plane means every mode decays. A zero eigenvalue is a free integrator, which drifts rather than settling. Purely imaginary eigenvalues are marginally stable and oscillate forever. A positive trace means the sum of eigenvalues is positive, so at least one eigenvalue has a positive real part, which is unstable.
